items.icaew-ai-standards::ai-strategy-policy: ICAEW's AI-governance guidance asks organisations to define an AI strategy aligned with business goals, and to put in place a communicated AI policy with supporting procedures. The policy should settle who is accountable overall for AI governance and risk, who brings the needed capabilities together, and what roles and responsibilities run across the whole AI system life cycle; it should be reviewed and communicated regularly as the technology and the organisation change.
items.icaew-ai-standards::risk-based-governanc: Governance of AI is not one-size-fits-all: ICAEW frames proportionate risk management as a board-level duty. Assessments should cover the inherent risk of each use case, including ethical impact assessments of fairness, autonomy and harm, societal implications beyond technical compliance, and the risk of non-compliance with law. A defined risk taxonomy keeps assessment consistent, management sets risk tolerances, the board approves the overall risk appetite, and third-party contributions to AI development and use are assessed like any other risk source.
items.icaew-ai-standards::oversight-and-monito: Where AI systems inform or make decisions affecting individuals, ICAEW expects the human role to be deliberately designed: intervention and override points sized to the risk, with override activity recorded, examined and used to improve the system. Because models can degrade silently as data and behaviour drift, organisations should run processes to monitor and oversee their AI systems, with protocols to detect performance degradation and to retrain where needed.
items.icaew-ai-standards::assurance-readiness: For higher-risk AI systems, ICAEW adds readiness questions drawn from its assurance perspective: outputs should be explicable to relevant internal and external stakeholders in business terms, with documented logic; input data should be complete, accurate, tested for bias and traceable to source, owner and validation date, with lineage and consent records; cyber controls should address AI-specific threats such as malicious content injected into training data, information leakage and unsafe generated code; and there should be clear procedures for reporting and handling significant AI failures or harmful outputs, including contractual liability terms and escalation routes.
